beads.title: An MDM-supplied AuthKey cannot enrol a node, because nothing reads the policy key
beads.description:
Go's `Start` resolves an auth key from three sources in order, and the third has no counterpart here. In `ipn/ipnlocal/local.go`, after `opts.AuthKey` and the `--config` file's `AuthKey` (including its `file:<path>` indirection) have both come up empty, and only when the node is not already `Running` and no config file is in use, it reads `pkey.AuthKey` from the policy client: `sysak, _ := b.polc.GetString(pkey.AuthKey, "")`. Two guards go with it, and both matter. A non-empty policy key is used only when there are no existing login profiles OR the state is `NeedsLogin` -- otherwise it logs "not setting opts.AuthKey from syspolicy; login profiles exist, state=%v" and leaves the node alone, so dropping a policy file on an already-enrolled host never silently re-registers it. And the value is `strings.TrimSpace`d before use, because an MDM payload that round-trips through a plist or a registry string arrives with a trailing newline more often than not. The point of the key is that it is the ONLY way an administrator enrols a fleet without touching each host: the same policy file that pins `Hostname` and `ExitNodeIP` also carries the credential that gets the node onto the tailnet in the first place.

This fork resolves the key and never reads it. `src/ipn/syspolicy.rs` defines `AuthKey` as a `ValueType::String`, types it, merges it and reports it through `tnet syspolicy list` like every other key, and the only by-name policy reads anywhere in the daemon are `EncryptState` and `HardwareAttestation` (`src/bin/tailnetd.rs`) plus the two always-on keys (`src/ipn/alwayson.rs`). The auth key reaches the engine from `tnet up --auth-key`, the `TS_AUTH_KEY` environment variable, or the `--config` source; a policy file that carries one changes nothing, and `tnet syspolicy list` prints it back to the administrator as though it were live. That is the same failure the syspolicy-application work just removed for prefs, still standing for the one key whose consumer is not a pref.

Three decisions. FIRST, secrecy: this daemon carries auth keys in `secrecy::SecretString` and keeps them out of logs and out of `status`, while the policy snapshot is a reporting surface -- `tnet syspolicy list` prints every configured key with its value and origin. Applying `AuthKey` means the snapshot now holds a credential, so either the report redacts this key by name or the loader keeps its value out of the snapshot and hands it straight to the login path. Decide it explicitly; the honest default is to redact in the report and say so in the column. SECOND, precedence: Go puts policy LAST, behind both the explicit flag and the config file, which is the opposite of how policy ranks for prefs -- an operator who typed a key meant that key. Keep Go's order, and note the inversion where the precedence rule for prefs is documented so the next reader does not read it as a bug. THIRD, the profiles guard: Go's condition is written against `len(b.pm.Profiles()) > 0` and `ipn.NeedsLogin`, and this fork derives "has this node ever been configured" from the existence of `prefs.json`; port the intent (never re-register a node that is already enrolled) rather than the literal expression.

beads.title: A policy-pinned exit node is silently overwritten instead of refused, and ExitNode.AllowOverride does nothing
beads.description:
Applying `ExitNodeIP` to prefs is only half of what Go does with an exit-node policy; the other half is a refusal, and this fork has neither it nor the key that relaxes it. In `ipn/ipnlocal/local.go`, `checkEditPrefsAccessLocked` runs before any prefs edit is applied: when the edit touches `ExitNodeID`, `ExitNodeIP` or `AutoExitNode` and `b.polc.HasAnyOf(pkey.ExitNodeID, pkey.ExitNodeIP)` reports the exit node is policy-managed, the edit is rejected with `exit node cannot be changed: managed by policy` (`errManagedByPolicy`). The one escape is `pkey.AllowExitNodeOverride` (`"ExitNode.AllowOverride"`, default false): with it set, a user may pick a DIFFERENT exit node, but `changeDisablesExitNodeLocked` still refuses any edit that would leave `ExitNodeID` empty, so an override can move the egress but never turn it off. When an override is allowed and taken, `onEditPrefsLocked` records it in `b.overrideExitNodePolicy`, which suppresses the policy re-apply on subsequent reconciles; `sysPolicyChanged` clears that flag whenever `ExitNodeID`, `ExitNodeIP` or `AllowExitNodeOverride` changes, and `onEditPrefsLocked` also clears it whenever the node connects or disconnects. So upstream's answer to "the administrator pinned an exit node and the user typed a different one" is a visible error by default and a remembered, bounded exemption when the administrator opted into one.

Here the same command line succeeds and then quietly does nothing. `syspolicy::apply_to_prefs` pins the exit-node selector from `ExitNodeIP`, and `Backend::reconcile_sys_policy` runs AFTER the caller's own overrides on every prefs write -- so `tnet set --exit-node=<peer>` under a pinning policy is accepted, reports success, and persists the administrator's node instead of the requested one. Nothing is printed and nothing distinguishes it from an edit that took effect. `ExitNode.AllowOverride` is defined in `src/ipn/syspolicy.rs` as a `ValueType::Boolean` and is read by nothing at all, so an administrator who sets it to allow user overrides gets exactly the behaviour they get when they leave it unset. The pair is the exit-node analogue of the always-on gate: the re-assert exists, the refusal does not.

Two decisions. WHERE the refusal lives: it belongs in the shared prefs pre-validation, before anything is mutated or persisted, alongside the always-on disconnect gate -- one place that both `up` and `set` reach, with `--config` deliberately below policy as the existing precedence ruling already has it. WHAT counts as "managed", given this fork refuses `ExitNodeID` rather than applying it: Go asks `HasAnyOf(ExitNodeID, ExitNodeIP)`, so a policy file naming only `ExitNodeID` still locks the pref upstream even though the value is unusable here. Refusing an operator's exit node on the strength of a key this build has already refused to honour would be the worst of both, so the defensible reading is to lock on the keys that are actually applied and to say so where the `ExitNodeID` refusal is documented. The override bookkeeping (`overrideExitNodePolicy`, and its two reset conditions) is the part to port last and to port whole, since an exemption that is never cleared is worse than one that never existed.

beads.title: A permitted always-on disconnect has no bounded window, because ReconnectAfter is never armed
beads.description:
Always-on mode upstream is a loop with three moving parts, and this fork ships one of them. The refusal gate is `ipnauth.CheckDisconnectPolicy`, which is ported. The re-assert is `applySysPolicy` forcing `WantRunning` back to true, which is ported. The part between them is not: in `ipn/ipnlocal/local.go`, `onEditPrefsLocked` fires whenever an edit takes `WantRunning` from true to false, sets `b.overrideAlwaysOn = true` so the re-assert stops fighting a disconnect the gate has already permitted, and then reads `pkey.ReconnectAfter` -- `if reconnectAfter, _ := b.polc.GetDuration(pkey.ReconnectAfter, 0); reconnectAfter > 0 { b.startReconnectTimerLocked(reconnectAfter) }`. `startReconnectTimerLocked` is careful in ways worth copying: it stops any previous timer, captures the current profile ID, and when it fires it re-checks both that it is still the live timer and that the profile has not changed before editing `WantRunning` back to true as `ipnauth.Self`, logging either `automatically reconnected as %q after %v` or the failure. `sysPolicyChanged` clears `overrideAlwaysOn` whenever `AlwaysOn.Enabled` or `AlwaysOn.OverrideWithReason` changes, so a policy edit revokes an outstanding exemption. The administrator's contract is therefore precise: a user with a reason may take the node down for exactly `ReconnectAfter` and no longer.

This fork has the key and not the mechanism. `src/ipn/syspolicy.rs` defines `ReconnectAfter` as a `ValueType::Duration` and parses it with the Go duration grammar, `tnet syspolicy list` renders it (`"60m"` prints as `1h0m0s`), and nothing reads it. There is no `overrideAlwaysOn` equivalent either, which both modules already admit in their own docs: a permitted disconnect stands until the next reconcile point -- daemon start, `up`, `set` or a `--config` reload -- and is undone there. So an administrator who writes `ReconnectAfter: 30m` gets an unbounded outage on a node nobody touches, and one who writes nothing gets a node that may pop back up at an arbitrary moment because someone ran an unrelated `tnet set`. Neither is the policy they configured.

Two decisions, in this order. FIRST, the override flag, which is the prerequisite and is worth landing even alone: without it the timer is pointless, because the re-assert can undo the disconnect before the timer ever fires. It has to be reset on the same three events Go resets it on -- a connect or disconnect, a profile switch, and a change to either always-on key -- and it is in-memory state, so decide explicitly what a daemon restart means (Go loses it too, and the node comes back up, which is the safe direction for a policy whose whole purpose is to keep the node on). SECOND, the timer's lifecycle: what cancels it (a manual `up`, a profile switch, a policy change), and what happens if the daemon is stopped while one is outstanding. The profile-ID guard is not incidental -- without it a timer armed under one profile reconnects a different one -- and this daemon has profile switching, so port it rather than simplify it.

beads.title: There is no LocalAPI shutdown verb, so AllowTailscaledRestart gates nothing
beads.description:
Upstream's LocalAPI can stop the daemon, and the policy key that authorises it is one this fork already resolves. `ipn/localapi/localapi.go` routes `"shutdown"` to `serveShutdown`, which is four refusals and one event: non-`POST` gets `only POST allowed` (405); a caller without write access gets `shutdown access denied` (403); a caller WITH write access still gets `shutdown access denied by policy` (403) unless `polc.GetBoolean(pkey.AllowTailscaledRestart, false)` is true; and only then does it write 200, flush, and publish a `localapi.Shutdown` event on the bus. `ipn/ipnserver/server.go` is the sole subscriber: it closes the LocalAPI listener, which unwinds `Run` and ends the process, so the service manager restarts it -- which is why the key is called AllowTailscaledRestart rather than AllowShutdown. The client half is `LocalClient.ShutdownTailscaled` (`POST /localapi/v0/shutdown`). The default is false, so this is opt-in: the shape is an administrator handing a management agent one specific, auditable power over the daemon without handing it root.

This fork has neither end. There is no `shutdown` variant in `Request` (`src/localapi.rs`), no dispatch arm in `src/server.rs`, and `AllowTailscaledRestart` is defined in `src/ipn/syspolicy.rs` as a `ValueType::Boolean` that nothing reads -- an administrator can set it, watch `tnet syspolicy list` echo it, and there is no operation for it to permit. Stopping `tailnetd` today means signalling the process or asking the service manager, both of which need privileges beyond LocalAPI write access, and neither of which the policy file can grant or withhold.

The decision is whether this fork wants the verb at all, and it should be made in writing either way, because the alternative to a ruling is that the next sweep re-finds the key. If yes: the refusal ORDER is the part to port exactly (method, then write access, then policy, each with its own message and status), since a caller has to be able to tell "you may not" from "nobody may", and the write-access check must come first so the policy state is not readable by an unauthorised caller. The mechanism is a clean graceful stop -- drop the listener, unwind the accept loop, let the existing shutdown path run -- and NOT a `process::exit`, so the state file, the socket and any live device close the way they do on SIGTERM. If no: say so where the key is defined and report it in the same unenforced-key channel that already carries `UnattendedMode`, so the report stops implying the key does something. Worth noting the asymmetry either way: this daemon ships `tnet install`/`uninstall` and writes the systemd unit and the launchd plist, so it already owns the restart story on both platforms this build targets, and the verb would slot into that rather than being a new concern.

beads.title: exit-node suggest ignores the administrator's AllowedSuggestedExitNodes list
beads.description:
`AllowedSuggestedExitNodes` is the policy key that tells a managed fleet which exit nodes it may be steered onto, and upstream threads it all the way into the picker. In `ipn/ipnlocal/local.go`, `fillAllowedSuggestions` reads it as a string array (`polc.GetStringArray`), turns it into a `set.Set[tailcfg.StableNodeID]`, and stores it behind `allowedSuggestedExitNodesMu`; `refreshAllowedSuggestions` rebuilds it at backend start and again from `sysPolicyChanged` whenever the key changes -- and that same callback immediately re-runs `SuggestExitNode`, so a policy edit re-picks the node rather than waiting for someone to ask. `getAllowedSuggestions` hands the set to `suggestExitNode`, which passes it to both ranking strategies, and the filter is applied to CANDIDATES before ranking: `if allowList != nil && !allowList.Contains(peer.StableID()) { continue }`. The nil-versus-empty distinction is load bearing -- an unset key is `nil` and means no restriction, while a configured empty array means nothing is allowed -- and because the filter runs before the DERP-latency ranking, the result is the best node the administrator permits rather than the best node overall filtered afterwards to nothing.

This fork resolves the key and never consults it. `src/ipn/syspolicy.rs` defines `AllowedSuggestedExitNodes` as a `ValueType::StringList`, validates it element by element (a bare string and a list holding a non-string are both refused with the Go-shaped type-mismatch message), and reports it. `Backend::suggest_exit_node` is a thin shim over the engine's `Device::suggest_exit_node()` (`src/ipn/diag.rs`), which returns one suggestion carrying a stable node id and a display name. So `tnet exit-node suggest` on a policy-managed node can and does recommend a node the administrator excluded, and the operator who follows the recommendation with `tnet set --exit-node=...` egresses through it.

The decision is how much of the filter is buildable on this side of the engine boundary, and the answer splits cleanly, so take the first half now and file the second. The daemon holds the returned stable id and the policy set, so it can already REFUSE to hand back a suggestion outside the allow-list -- an honest empty result, which is what Go returns when no candidate passes, and which is strictly better than recommending a forbidden node. What it cannot do is re-rank: choosing the best ALLOWED node needs the candidate list and the DERP latencies the engine ranks on, so an allow-list that excludes only the engine's top pick yields no suggestion here where Go yields the runner-up. That is an engine ask (an allow-list argument on `suggest_exit_node`, or a candidate enumeration the daemon can rank itself), and it should be filed against `docs/ENGINE_ASKS.md` rather than worked around by re-implementing the ranking. Port the nil-versus-empty rule exactly while in there: an unset key must not become an empty allow-list that suppresses every suggestion.

beads.title: The policy snapshot never reaches the notify bus, so a watcher cannot see policy change
beads.description:
Upstream treats the effective policy as part of the backend state a client watches, not as something a client polls for. `ipn/backend.go` declares `NotifySysPolicyChanges NotifyWatchOpt = 1 << 17`, documented as causing "the first Notify message, which is sent immediately, to contain the current effective [setting.Snapshot] in [Notify.Policy]", with `Notify.Policy` "included in subsequent messages whenever the effective policy changes" and delivered as a full snapshot every time rather than a delta. The backend side is two pieces in `ipn/ipnlocal/local.go`: the initial-state assembly fills `ini.Policy` from `b.polc.GetPolicySnapshot("")` when the mask bit is set, and the same watch registers a policy change callback for the life of the session (`RegisterChangeCallback`, unregistered on exit) whose handler `sysPolicyChangedForSession` fetches a fresh snapshot and sends it to that one session. The bit is part of the mask a LocalAPI `WatchIPNBus` caller may request, so a GUI or a management agent learns that the administrator changed something at the moment it happens.

This fork has the watch and not the bit. `Request::Watch` (`src/localapi.rs`) carries `initial_state`, `initial_netmap` and a prefs flag -- the first two threaded to the engine's `NotifyWatchOpt`, the third daemon-built -- and `NotifyView` has no policy field. The policy snapshot is readable only by asking for it: `tnet syspolicy list` and the `syspolicy reload` verb, both one-shot reads. A watcher therefore cannot distinguish "policy unchanged" from "policy changed and I have not asked again", which matters more here than upstream now that policy outranks local prefs on every write: a `tnet set` that appears to do nothing is explained by a policy the watcher cannot see.

Two decisions. FIRST, what "on change" means when the only source is a JSON file read at startup and re-read on an explicit `syspolicy reload`. There is no registry watcher here and nothing to subscribe to, so the honest MVP is the initial snapshot plus a push on every reload -- which is a real change signal, just a coarser one -- and the mask bit's documentation should say so rather than promise a watch this build cannot perform. Whether to add a file watcher is a separate, larger question and should not be smuggled in with the wire change. SECOND, the wire shape: this fork's reporting surface is a flat list of per-key origin/value/error rows, and the notify field should carry exactly that rather than invent a second rendering of the same snapshot -- and it must inherit whatever redaction rule the report settles on for credential-bearing keys, because a notify stream is read by more processes than a CLI is. Note this also answers, in Go's own shape, the open question about making unenforceable-key warnings visible beyond the daemon log: the snapshot is the thing that gets pushed, so the refusal belongs on the row rather than in a new channel.
